playbook.title: High-volume billing operations
playbook.text: T6 High-volume billing. A provider files far more claims, and receives far more reimbursement, than peers of the same type. Volume alone is not evidence of fraud, because large hospitals legitimately bill more, so a volume flag should be compared against size-adjusted measures before escalation. Signals are total claims, total reimbursement, inpatient claim counts and the number of beneficiaries.

playbook.title: Upcoding to a more complex or expensive service
playbook.text: T4 Upcoding. The provider bills a more complex or costly service than the one performed, for example a higher-paying diagnosis-related group for an inpatient stay. Signals are reimbursement per claim and per beneficiary well above peers, a high maximum inpatient payment, long stays relative to peers, and a wide spread of diagnosis-related groups per inpatient claim.

playbook.title: Excessive length of stay
playbook.text: T7 Excessive inpatient stays. Admissions are extended beyond clinical need to raise payment, or stays are billed for longer than they lasted. Signals are mean and maximum length of stay and the share of stays of ten days or more, compared with inpatient peers.

playbook.title: Billing for services not provided
playbook.text: T1 Billing for services not provided (phantom billing). The provider submits claims for visits, admissions or procedures that never took place. Typical traces are claims for patients who had died, many claims per patient with no change in diagnosis, and unusually high claim counts relative to the number of attending physicians who could have delivered the care. In this dataset no claim is dated after a beneficiary's death, so the death check cannot fire; the usable signals are claims per beneficiary and claims per attending physician.

playbook.title: Duplicate submission of a claim
playbook.text: T2 Duplicate claims. The same service is billed twice, either by the same provider or by two providers, often with the same patient, date, diagnosis and amount. Signals are the share of a provider's claims that match another claim on patient, start date, first diagnosis code and amount, separately for matches within the provider and across providers.
